text: This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a draft paragraph in which the writer discusses automated academic feedback, citation practice, section logic, evidence use, and revision decisions. The text is de-identified, uses invented authors and generic study contexts, and contains no classroom participant data. The specific issue is that the paragraph writes Smith 2020 and Brown 2021 without author date punctuation, so the system should bind feedback to APA narrative and parenthetical citation rules rather than give generic polishing advice.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a literature review paragraph about feedback systems, revision depth, and classroom analytics. The paragraph is de-identified and uses invented sources. It alternates between Lee stated, according to Chen, and parenthetical markers without a stable author date pattern. The feedback should identify inconsistent citation form and distinguish the writer's synthesis from source claims. A grounded answer should cite the APA norm node and the traceability node instead of inventing a new formatting rule.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a draft paragraph that uses numbered citations in a thesis discussion. The text says previous work [1] and later studies [2] support the same conclusion, but it never identifies author, title, year, or source type. The paragraph also mixes numbered citation markers with informal author mentions. The expected feedback should focus on GB style bibliography traceability and should not merely complain about tone or grammar because the main problem is reference completeness.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph about knowledge graph feedback and student revision. The writer places one citation at the end of six sentences even though the sentences make separate historical, empirical, and design claims. The citation may support one claim but cannot reasonably cover the whole paragraph. The system should detect citation scope rather than invent missing sources. A valid feedback item should bind to the broad citation scope node and the empirical claim source node.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a thesis paragraph in which the author reports that automated comments improve final scores by a precise percentage. The statistical claim has no source immediately after it, while a later sentence cites a general dashboard paper. The expected feedback should state that empirical or quantitative claims require specific and verifiable sources. It should not mark the whole paragraph as unusable because the topic and structure are otherwise coherent.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a review paragraph with several invented studies. The writer paraphrases a study but changes the scope from a small engineering writing class to all university writing courses. The citation exists, but the evidence is being overstretched. The system should produce feedback about preserving source meaning and avoiding unsupported generalization. The answer should cite evidence integration and traceability norms, not simply demand another reference list entry.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph using both APA author date citations and numbered references. The paragraph is not wrong because it cites sources, but the mixed style makes it unclear which convention the thesis follows. The expected feedback should ask for one consistent citation strategy and complete source traceability. It should avoid claiming that every citation is fabricated. This checks whether the system can give bounded, citation-bound feedback instead of overcorrecting.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a literature paragraph where every sentence begins with researchers say or studies show. The paragraph gives no concrete author, date, or numbered source for those claims. The expected feedback should focus on attaching empirical claims to verifiable sources and improving reader traceability. A grounded system output should include a REF tag for the claim source norm and should avoid treating this as a section order problem because the section location is not the issue.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes an abstract that begins with implementation details, then reports interface functions, and only later mentions the educational problem. The order makes the purpose hard to identify because readers see a solution before the problem and objective. The expected feedback should bind to abstract sequence rules and element order problems. It should not invent missing experimental results; the correct response is to reorganize the abstract into problem, objective, method, evaluation, and contribution.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes an introduction that lists login, dashboard, retrieval, and graph display features. The paragraph reads like a product manual and does not establish why generic writing feedback is insufficient. The expected feedback should identify the missing research gap and explain that contribution statements should respond to the gap. It should not focus on button labels or interface wording because the section-level problem is motivation and contribution positioning.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a method section that first claims the proposed system outperforms baselines, then returns to describe the query set, threshold, and scoring procedure. This mixes procedure with interpretation and makes the experiment hard to reproduce. The expected feedback should cite IMRAD separation and result placement norms. It should not produce a generic suggestion to improve flow because the problem is the boundary between method and result sections.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a results section that repeats implementation details about the workbench, sidebar, and streaming interface. It does not report measured outcomes, pass rates, latency values, traceability statistics, or comparison against baselines. The expected feedback should cite the results reporting node and evaluation metric node. It should not praise the detailed interface description because the section title promises evidence produced by the experiment.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a conclusion that introduces a new claim about reducing teacher workload across all writing courses. The preceding experiment only evaluated traceability on a fixed query set. The conclusion also omits limitations about synthetic data and expert review. The expected feedback should cite conclusion synthesis and limitation boundaries. A valid response should narrow the claim instead of expanding it into an unsupported teaching effectiveness statement.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes an abstract that includes the problem, method, and contribution but omits any evaluation evidence. Readers cannot tell whether the system was tested, what metric was used, or whether feedback traceability was measured. The expected feedback should ask for a compact evaluation element in the abstract and bind to the abstract structure node. It should not demand classroom learning outcomes because the experiment may only support system validation.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes an introduction that states the system has many modules and then immediately moves to technical architecture. The paragraph never explains the limitation of non-grounded feedback or why provenance validation is the research contribution. The expected feedback should connect background, problem, gap, and contribution. It should avoid treating the paragraph as merely too long because the structural issue is missing rhetorical movement.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a discussion section that only repeats the main numeric result without explaining why graph expansion changed validation behavior. The paragraph gives the outcome but no mechanism, implication, or constraint. The expected feedback should cite discussion interpretation and mechanism explanation nodes. It should not invent new data or claim student learning improvement. The correct feedback is to interpret measured traceability results within the stated experiment boundary.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a background paragraph that immediately lists Redis, endpoint names, and frontend panels before explaining the educational context. Readers do not learn why students need norm-bound feedback or why generic comments are risky. The expected feedback should cite the background paragraph node and the paragraph function order node. It should not criticize citation style because the main issue is that implementation details appear before context and problem framing.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a method paragraph that claims the feedback is clear and useful but does not describe the query set, model configuration, threshold, annotation process, or metric calculation. The expected feedback should cite method reproducibility and IMRAD separation. It should not accept evaluative claims inside the method paragraph. A grounded response should recommend adding procedural details before any result interpretation.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a result paragraph that reports a pass rate, then explains graph expansion mechanics, then makes a broad classroom implication. The sentence roles shift from result to method to discussion without a stable topic sentence. The expected feedback should cite result paragraph and topic sentence norms. It should not ask for more citations as the first correction because the paragraph function is the primary problem.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a discussion paragraph that repeats the same threshold pass rate three times. It does not explain why low confidence references decreased or how validation changes interpretation. The expected feedback should cite discussion interpretation and mechanism explanation nodes. It should avoid inventing a new experiment. The target behavior is to recommend a bounded explanation of mechanisms, implications, and constraints based on existing results.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a limitation paragraph that says the system is scalable, convenient, and suitable for all writing courses. It briefly mentions synthetic data but immediately treats current evidence as enough for broad teaching value. The expected feedback should cite limitation paragraph and evidence boundary nodes. It should recommend stating what the study cannot prove, why the limitation matters, and what future work should test.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph that should introduce the research problem but instead compares three implementation libraries. The sentences are grammatical, but they do not perform the expected background or problem framing function. The expected feedback should bind to paragraph background and function order norms. It should avoid marking the paragraph as factually wrong because the issue is rhetorical function rather than factual content.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a method paragraph where the first sentence gives a topic, but later sentences drift into recommendations for teachers and interface design implications. The procedure is only briefly mentioned. The expected feedback should cite method reproducibility and topic alignment. It should recommend keeping procedure, configuration, data, and metrics together. It should not claim that the paragraph has no value, because some useful procedural content is present.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a result paragraph with numbers but no comparison or concise interpretation. It says one method scored higher but does not tell readers which baseline is meaningful or what the difference implies. The expected feedback should cite result paragraph norms and evaluation metric norms. It should avoid broad claims about classroom adoption. The revision should add a bounded comparison and a short interpretation tied to measured outcomes.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph that claims traceable feedback increases student trust, then lists retrieved node counts without explaining how the counts support the trust claim. The evidence and reasoning are disconnected. The expected feedback should cite claim evidence reasoning and interpretation norms. It should not simply request another citation, because the problem is the missing reasoning bridge between the measured system output and the broader argument.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph that reports full GraphRAG has a higher pass rate, then concludes that all students will write better after using the system. The conclusion is stronger than the evidence because the experiment only measures groundedness. The expected feedback should cite limitation boundaries and cautious interpretation. It should clearly separate system verification from learning effect claims and avoid overstating instructional outcomes.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph where the topic sentence argues that graph expansion improves provenance validation. The following sentences only explain interface screenshots and do not return to validation, references, or groundedness. The expected feedback should cite topic alignment and claim evidence reasoning nodes. It should recommend replacing interface description with evidence about retrieved nodes, threshold passes, or error reduction.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph that lists three findings from different methods but never compares them or explains what pattern they reveal. Readers see numbers but no argumentative synthesis. The expected feedback should cite reasoning and discussion interpretation norms. It should ask the writer to explain whether validator, graph expansion, or retrieval quality accounts for the differences, without inventing unmeasured causes.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a discussion that states the proposed approach is reliable because it is advanced. The reasoning is circular and does not connect reliability to measurable outcomes such as valid references or false alarm rates. The expected feedback should cite claim evidence reasoning and objective academic style norms. It should recommend replacing promotional reasoning with traceability evidence and an explicit boundary for what reliability means.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a limitation section that acknowledges synthetic queries but then dismisses the limitation by saying the benchmark fully represents academic writing. That move weakens the argument because it names a limitation without accepting its consequence. The expected feedback should cite limitation boundaries and cautious style. It should advise the writer to report the benchmark as system validation rather than comprehensive classroom evidence.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a literature review that stacks five invented findings in sequence but never compares their methods, contexts, or implications. The citations exist, yet the paragraph does not synthesize evidence. The expected feedback should bind to evidence synthesis and claim evidence reasoning nodes. It should not count citations alone as sufficient because grounded academic feedback should distinguish source presence from meaningful integration.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph where one study about short-term revision comments is used to support a claim about long-term writing development. The source may be relevant but the interpretation exceeds the evidence. The expected feedback should cite paraphrase meaning preservation and cautious language norms. It should avoid accusing the writer of fabrication. The correct correction is to narrow the claim or add stronger evidence.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph that says the system improved usability, but the only evidence provided is a latency measurement. The evidence does not support the usability claim. The expected feedback should cite claim evidence reasoning and evidence integration norms. It should recommend either changing the claim to performance or adding expert review evidence for usability, while keeping the feedback bounded to available data.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph that quotes a guideline idea but does not explain how the guideline applies to the student's draft. The evidence appears as an isolated authority rather than integrated support for a specific critique. The expected feedback should cite evidence synthesis and actionable reasoning norms. It should recommend connecting the norm to the sentence-level problem and the revision action instead of adding more raw quotations.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a review paragraph that treats two studies with different participant groups as if they prove the same conclusion. The draft needs comparison and boundary language. The expected feedback should cite synthesis and cautious style norms. It should not invent exact sample sizes or study details. The answer should tell the writer to compare contexts, qualify the shared conclusion, and keep evidence tied to source scope.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph where the writer paraphrases a source as saying all automated feedback is accurate, although the invented source only discussed reduced surface errors. The expected feedback should cite paraphrase meaning preservation and empirical claim source norms. It should not only fix wording; it should identify the evidence distortion and recommend narrowing the paraphrase to what the source can support.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph that says the proposed platform is revolutionary, perfect, and obviously superior to existing teaching tools. The claims are promotional and not tied to evidence. The expected feedback should cite objective academic style and cautious claim norms. It should recommend replacing promotional adjectives with measured outcomes and bounded interpretation. It should not claim the technical system itself is invalid.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph claiming the benchmark proves the system will work in every course. The evidence is a local traceability test, so the wording should be more cautious. The expected feedback should cite hedging and limitation boundary norms. It should recommend using terms such as suggests, indicates, or in this benchmark rather than universal claims. The response should not demand new classroom data as if it already exists.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a discussion paragraph that alternates between careful metric reporting and marketing phrases such as extremely powerful and universally useful. The expected feedback should cite objective style and discussion interpretation norms. It should not erase all evaluative language; it should ask the writer to connect evaluation to measured outcomes and qualify claims that exceed the experiment.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph that asserts students definitely prefer citation-bound feedback, although the study only plans an expert review. The expected feedback should cite cautious style and evidence boundaries. It should recommend writing that expert review may indicate perceived usefulness, not student preference or learning improvement. This tests whether the system avoids turning pilot evaluation language into a stronger educational claim.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph where the writer says our method crushes baseline systems and guarantees cleaner writing. The tone is informal and the guarantee is unsupported. The expected feedback should cite objective academic style and empirical claim norms. It should recommend replacing informal comparison with measured metric differences and explain which claim is supported. The feedback should not remove all authorial stance, only unsupported promotional stance.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph that uses careful citation form but states that all previous systems fail because they lack graphs. The claim is too absolute and not supported by the cited evidence. The expected feedback should cite cautious language and claim evidence reasoning. It should avoid treating citation formatting as the main issue because the stronger problem is overgeneralized academic style.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph that says traceable feedback may support revision when students compare comments with explicit norms. The claim is cautious and cites a source, but the paragraph could explain the mechanism more fully. This is an ambiguous case: light suggestion is acceptable, but strong corrective feedback would be overcorrection. The expected response should be bounded, cite interpretation or claim evidence norms only if it gives a cautious recommendation, and avoid declaring the paragraph incorrect.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes an abstract that includes problem, method, and contribution but reports evaluation only briefly. The abstract is not clearly wrong, yet a reviewer might ask for a more concrete metric. This is an ambiguous case where the system should avoid harsh correction. A grounded response may cite the abstract structure node and suggest adding one evaluation phrase, but it should not mark the draft as structurally invalid.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a paragraph with one broad citation near the end, but the paragraph is a high-level synthesis rather than a list of separate empirical claims. A strong system should be cautious. It may suggest clarifying citation scope if the claims become more specific, but it should not assert a definite citation error. The expected reference node is citation scope because that is the relevant borderline norm.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a limitation paragraph that is short but honest. It says the query set is synthetic and future work should include classroom review. The paragraph could expand why the limitation matters, but it should not be treated as promotional or misleading. A cautious feedback system may cite the limitation node and suggest one explanatory sentence. A false alarm would claim that the paragraph hides the limitation.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a discussion paragraph that offers a plausible mechanism for graph expansion but does not include every metric. The discussion is acceptable if the results table already contains the numbers. The system should not demand repeated statistics in every paragraph. It may suggest linking the mechanism to one key metric. This tests whether feedback remains grounded and avoids unnecessary correction on borderline discussion quality.

This synthetic academic writing sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a literature paragraph that compares two invented systems and cites both. The synthesis is basic but present. The system may recommend more explicit comparison, but it should not say the paragraph lacks evidence integration entirely. A grounded answer should cite the evidence synthesis node only for a mild improvement suggestion. This item measures whether the feedback model can avoid exaggerated critique.

This synthetic academic writing control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It presents a coherent abstract that states the educational problem, the objective, the GraphRAG method, the evaluation dimensions, and the contribution. It uses cautious wording and does not claim classroom learning gains. Citations are not required in this short abstract fragment. A well-behaved system should avoid corrective feedback and may at most acknowledge that the structure is clear. This control item measures false alarms on acceptable academic writing.

This synthetic academic writing control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a method paragraph with the query set, method conditions, validation threshold, and metric calculation. It keeps procedure separate from interpretation and does not report results before the method is defined. The paragraph is de-identified and contains no participant data. A correct system should not invent a missing issue. It may recognize that the paragraph supports reproducibility without requiring additional unsupported classroom claims.

This synthetic academic writing control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It reports that grounded reference precision is a system validation metric and explicitly states that the metric does not prove student learning gains. The paragraph separates technical evidence from educational claims. It uses cautious wording and avoids promotional language. A well-grounded feedback system should not flag this as overclaiming. This item is a hard control because it mentions learning effects while clearly denying that they were proven.

This synthetic academic writing control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a limitation paragraph that acknowledges synthetic query data, compact knowledge graph size, and the absence of a classroom intervention. It then proposes future expert review and classroom deployment as separate work. The paragraph performs the limitation function correctly and does not hide the boundary of the evidence. The expected behavior is no correction, because the limitation is explicit, cautious, and aligned with the experimental design.

This synthetic academic writing control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It presents a results paragraph that reports four methods under the same query set and names the metrics used for comparison. It does not overinterpret the result and does not claim student improvement. The paragraph briefly explains why lower hallucinated reference rate matters for traceability. A correct system should accept the result function and avoid adding unnecessary citation or structure criticism.

This synthetic academic writing control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It discusses why graph expansion may retrieve adjacent norm nodes and why validation filters unsupported references. The paragraph links mechanism to measured groundedness metrics while preserving the system validation boundary. It uses cautious wording and does not introduce new claims. A feedback system should not treat every mention of graph expansion as requiring additional evidence if the paragraph is already bounded and coherent.

This synthetic academic writing control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes an introduction that moves from the difficulty of norm-based academic writing feedback to the risk of ungrounded model suggestions, then introduces provenance validation as the contribution. The structure follows background, problem, gap, and contribution. It does not list interface features before motivation. A correct system should avoid false alarms and may only provide optional polishing if asked.

This synthetic academic writing control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It describes a literature review paragraph that compares feedback systems by evidence source, traceability support, and validation mechanism. The paragraph uses generic invented citations consistently and does not overstate what those sources prove. It synthesizes the comparison rather than listing unrelated findings. The expected behavior is no corrective feedback, because citation, evidence integration, and argument coherence are all acceptable for this benchmark context.

This synthetic academic writing adversarial control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It includes bracketed mathematical ranges such as x in [0, L] and parameter options [low, medium, high]. These brackets are not citation markers and should not be treated as missing references. The paragraph is otherwise coherent and cautious. A robust system should avoid hallucinated citation feedback. This item specifically tests whether the evaluator and generation system confuse bracket notation with citation requirements.

This synthetic academic writing adversarial control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It contains a literal example of the required output pattern, for instance the instruction says feedback may cite [REF:node_id] when a norm is actually used. The text is explaining a format and is not itself making an unsupported academic claim. A robust system should not treat the placeholder as a hallucinated citation or force a real node reference. This case checks validator false acceptance and false rejection behavior.

This synthetic academic writing adversarial control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It mentions invented author names in an example sentence, but the paragraph explicitly says the names are placeholders for demonstrating citation syntax. The purpose is instructional, not a literature claim. A feedback system should not accuse the writer of missing bibliography entries. The correct behavior is to recognize the example context and avoid overcorrection while preserving the general citation guideline if needed.

This synthetic academic writing adversarial control sample is designed for provenance evaluation. It uses terms such as source, evidence, and citation while describing the benchmark design itself. The paragraph does not present external empirical claims and does not need a citation for every occurrence of those words. A robust feedback system should not trigger citation correction solely from vocabulary. This item measures false positive behavior when surface terms resemble citation problems but the rhetorical function is methodological explanation.
